document_check.note: The document is Mo W, Liu X, Yamakawa M, et al. 'Prevalence of sleep disturbances in people with mild cognitive impairment: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Psychiatry Research 339 (2024) 116067. The review cites it as Mo et al. 2024 for geographical region as a moderator. The document reports a region subgroup test (df = 3, Q = 34.025, p < 0.001) next to a measurement-method test (df = 2, Q = 30.173, p < 0.001), so author, year, design and cited result all match.

cited_result: Subgroup analysis of pooled subjective sleep-disturbance prevalence in MCI by geographical region: North America 19.1% (95% CI 14.7-23.6), Europe 40.9%, Asia 39.4%, Oceania 45.2%; between-subgroup Q = 34.025, df = 3, p < 0.001 (Table 3, p. 12-13). The review presents it as a moderator as strong as measurement method (Q = 30.173, df = 2).
tool_reason: The cited result is a subgroup (moderator) finding from a systematic review and meta-analysis of prevalence studies, so ROBIS applies.

domains.rationale: The protocol was registered and published, the criteria are explicit and fit a prevalence question, the restrictions (no case-control studies, no MMSE-only diagnosis) come with reasons, and there were no restrictions on language or date.

signalling.question: 1.1 Did the review adhere to pre-defined objectives and eligibility criteria?
signalling.quote: We registered our review protocol with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42022366108). This review was also conducted in accordance with a published protocol (Mo et al., 2023).

signalling.question: 1.2 Were the eligibility criteria appropriate for the review question?
signalling.quote: Studies were eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria: (1) included individuals with MCI as the primary study group; (2) reported sleep disturbances using a validated instrument, including subjective (e.g., the PSQI or NPI) and/or objective (e.g., polysomnography or actigraphy-based assessment) measures; (3) included individuals with a clinical diagnosis of MCI obtained using standardized diagnostic criteria; and (4) reported the sleep disturbance prevalence in people with MCI.

signalling.question: 1.3 Were eligibility criteria unambiguous?
signalling.quote: In the present study, sleep disturbances include long and short sleep duration, poor sleep quality, decreased SE, difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, early awakenings, increased number and length of awakenings, and excessive daytime sleepiness.

signalling.question: 1.4 Were all restrictions in eligibility criteria based on study characteristics appropriate?
signalling.quote: We did not include case–control studies because they cannot provide any information about the prevalence or incidence of a disease, as no measurements are made in a population-based sample

signalling.question: 1.5 Were any restrictions in eligibility criteria based on sources of information appropriate?
signalling.quote: searched from inception to January 20, 2024, with no restriction on the publication date or language.

domains.rationale: A librarian helped search six databases. The reference lists of included articles were hand-searched, authors were contacted, there were no language restrictions (non-English articles were translated), and two reviewers screened independently.

signalling.question: 2.1 Did the search include an appropriate range of databases/electronic sources for published and unpublished reports?
signalling.quote: the MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Elsevier), Cochrane Library (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials), Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (EBSCOhost), PsycINFO (EBSCOhost), and Web of Science (Clarivate) databases were searched from inception to January 20, 2024

signalling.question: 2.2 Were methods additional to database searching used to identify relevant reports?
signalling.quote: The reference lists of all included full-text articles were hand-searched to identify any additional relevant studies missed in the initial search.

signalling.question: 2.3 Were the terms and structure of the search strategy likely to retrieve as many eligible studies as possible?
signalling.quote: In collaboration with an experienced librarian, ... The full search strategy is detailed in the supplementary materials.

signalling.question: 2.4 Were restrictions based on date, publication format, or language appropriate?
signalling.quote: with no restriction on the publication date or language. ... We translated non-English articles to determine their eligibility.

signalling.question: 2.5 Were efforts made to minimise error in selection of studies?
signalling.quote: Titles and abstracts were assessed by two independent reviewers (M.W and L.X) against the inclusion criteria for the review. The full texts of selected citations were assessed in detail against the inclusion criteria by the same two independent reviewers.

domains.rationale: Two reviewers extracted data independently with a standard JBI tool and appraised the studies in duplicate with the JBI prevalence checklist. Study characteristics are tabulated. The one weakness is that the checklist was reduced to a summed score, which was used to exclude studies.

signalling.question: 3.1 Were efforts made to minimise error in data collection?
signalling.quote: Two independent reviewers (M.W and L.X) extracted data from the studies included in the review using the standardized JBI data extraction tool for assessing prevalence and incidence.

signalling.question: 3.2 Were sufficient study characteristics available for both review authors and readers to be able to interpret the results?
signalling.quote: The characteristics of the included studies are described in Table 1.

signalling.question: 3.3 Were all relevant study results collected for use in the synthesis?
signalling.quote: If a publication involved longitudinal assessment, only the baseline data were extracted.

signalling.question: 3.4 Was risk of bias (or methodological quality) formally assessed using appropriate criteria?
signalling.quote: critically appraised eligible studies for methodological quality using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Studies Reporting Prevalence Data (Munn et al., 2015). ... The positive responses were summed, with the maximum score being 9 points

signalling.question: 3.5 Were efforts made to minimise error in risk of bias assessment?
signalling.quote: Two independent reviewers (M.W and L.X) critically appraised eligible studies ... Any disagreements were resolved through discussion with a third senior reviewer (M.Y).

domains.rationale: The region comparison is a set of univariable subgroup tests on pooled estimates that mix different instruments and case definitions. Heterogeneity within each region is very high (I2 89-98%). Region is not separable from measurement method: every North American study listed with a subjective tool in Table 1 used an informant scale (NPI-12, NPI-Q or BRSD), and informant-rated prevalence (23.7%) is much lower than self-report (49.4%). Region is also entangled with setting (Europe is mostly clinic-based). Nothing adjusts for these, and robustness checks cover only the overall pooled estimate. The document does not say whether the region subgroup was pre-specified.

signalling.question: 4.1 Did the synthesis include all studies that it should?
signalling.quote: Data synthesis was performed only for studies of fair (overall score, 4–6) and good (overall score, 7–9) methodological quality. ... Because only one study each was conducted in Africa and South America, and only one straddled multiple continents, meta-analysis of these studies was not possible

signalling.question: 4.2 Were all pre-defined analyses reported or departures explained?
signalling.quote: Searched the Methods and the stated research questions for a list of planned subgroups. The only statement is 'Subgroup analyses were used to explore potential sources of heterogeneity.' (p. 3), and the research questions name only clinic- versus community-based and subjective versus objective measures (p. 2). The published protocol is cited but its content is not reported, so it cannot be established whether geographical region was pre-specified.

signalling.question: 4.3 Was the synthesis appropriate given the nature and similarity in the research questions, study designs and outcomes across included studies?
signalling.quote: it is important to acknowledge that the lack of equivalence across studies in the sleep measurement instruments used hampers our ability to draw conclusions regarding the global prevalence of sleep disturbance in people with MCI.

signalling.question: 4.4 Was between-study variation (heterogeneity) minimal or addressed in the synthesis?
signalling.quote: In the region of Europe covered by this study, clinic-based studies were approximately four times more prevalent than community-based studies, which may have contributed to the high prevalence of sleep disturbances.

signalling.question: 4.5 Were the findings robust, e.g. as demonstrated through funnel plot or sensitivity analyses?
signalling.quote: Egger's regression test revealed significant publication bias (t = 5.23, p < 0.001). ... Sensitivity analysis, performed using random effects models to determine the effect of individual studies on the pooled sleep disturbance prevalence estimates, showed no significant changes upon the removal of any single study (Fig. 6).

signalling.question: 4.6 Were biases in primary studies minimal or addressed in the synthesis?
signalling.quote: We combined the data from the meta-analyses and examined the effects of publication year, participant age, percentage of females, and study quality; none of these covariates significantly moderated the estimated sleep disturbance prevalence

domains.domain: Phase 3: Risk of bias in the review
domains.rationale: The authors mention the European clinic-sample imbalance and the non-equivalent instruments. They still explain the North American result with untested contextual reasons rather than the measurement-method overlap. The conclusion also credits data source with contributing to heterogeneity even though that subgroup test was non-significant.

signalling.question: A. Did the interpretation of findings address all of the concerns identified in Domains 1 to 4?
signalling.quote: In contrast, North America prioritizes sleep medicine, with robust government support, strict professional guidelines, and extensive research and education initiatives likely explaining why it had the lowest prevalence of sleep disturbances.

signalling.question: B. Was the relevance of identified studies to the review's research question appropriately considered?
signalling.quote: Fourth, studies from low-income countries were lacking.

signalling.question: C. Did the reviewers avoid emphasising results on the basis of their statistical significance?
signalling.quote: Moreover, variations in the data source and sleep disturbance assessment method contributed to the notable heterogeneity in the literature concerning sleep disturbance prevalence in individuals with MCI.

overall: High risk of bias (for the geographical-region moderator result)
overall_rationale: The search, selection, extraction and appraisal (domains 1-3) are sound, so the overall pooled prevalence is reasonably well founded. The cited moderator result is not. It comes from unadjusted subgroup comparisons, within-subgroup I2 of 89-98%, and region overlaps measurement method and setting (every North American subjective study listed used an informant scale). Whether it was pre-specified is not reported, and the interpretation does not resolve the overlap.

applicability.rationale: The review targets people with a clinical or criteria-based MCI diagnosis, which matches the synthesis population. The region finding applies only to subjective (self-, informant- or clinician-rated) prevalence.
